bib.title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution", Liyan Tang, Cyrus Rashtchian, Chun-Sung Ferng, Andrew Tomkins, Da-Cheng Juan, Tu Vu (Google Research; Virginia Tech). arXiv:2608.27454v1 [cs.AI], 27 Aug 2026 (preprint).
COVERAGE: All 28 pages read, 86,717 chars extracted, including appendices A-E (algorithm, dataset splits, implementation, baselines, API-call analysis, system prompts). The reference list was skimmed. Figure captions script printed nothing; captions were taken from the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The persistent wiki is what drives the gain. Removing the wiki and the Wiki Maintainer from the Skill Proposer drops average accuracy by 15 points.
  number: 48.7 -> 63.7 average
  setup: Gemini-3.5-Flash; LiveMath, SealQA, SpreadSheet, OfficeQA (ALFWorld is absent from Table 3); default config = proposer has wiki, inference agent does not. The no-wiki row removes the Maintainer, so no accumulation across iterations.
  quote: "providing the Skill Proposer with access to the persistent wiki increases average benchmark performance from 48.7% to 63.7% (+15.0%), with substantial gains on LiveMath (51.3% to 72.6%) and SpreadsheetBench (49.9% to 76.6%)."
  where: p.11, Sec 5.1, Table 3
- claim: Giving the inference agent wiki access during training rollouts hurts the evolved skills.
  number: 63.7 -> 60.9 average; LiveMath 72.6 -> 64.8
  setup: Same ablation as above. The authors' explanation is a hypothesis, not tested.
  quote: "providing the Inference Agent with wiki access during training rollouts reduces average benchmark performance from 63.7% to 60.9%, with a substantial drop on LiveMath from 72.6% to 64.8%. We hypothesize that ... some task-solving knowledge may be obtained directly from the wiki rather than the skills, which can make the resulting trajectories less informative for skill development."
  where: p.11
- claim: WikiSkill has the highest average of the methods compared on all five models.
  number: margins over the best baseline of +3.3, +5.1, +10.0, +5.8, +12.0 points
  setup: 5 benchmarks, 5 models, empty initial skill set, full skill text injected into the system prompt. Scores are averages of 3 independent evolution runs. Paired bootstrap, 1,000 iterations, p<0.05. Baselines are Trace2Skill, EvoSkill and SkillOpt. The tables show no variance across runs, and the validation splits are small.
  quote: "WikiSkill improves average performance by 3.3, 5.1, 10.0, 5.8, and 12.0 points for Qwen-3.5-4B, Qwen-3.5-9B, Qwen-3.6-27B, Gemma-4-31B, and Gemini-3.5-Flash, respectively."
  where: p.7, Table 1
  Table 1 averages (No skill / Trace2Skill / EvoSkill / SkillOpt / WikiSkill):
    Qwen-3.5-4B: 26.2 / 32.1 / 33.7 / 35.2 / 38.5
    Qwen-3.5-9B: 29.9 / 36.7 / 42.3 / 40.2 / 47.4
    Qwen-3.6-27B: 39.4 / 47.3 / 53.3 / 50.7 / 63.3
    Gemma-4-31B: 41.3 / 45.8 / 43.4 / 49.1 / 54.9
    Gemini-3.5-Flash: 49.5 / 55.6 / 56.1 / 55.9 / 68.1
- claim: Gains from skill evolution grow with model size, and a small model with skills can beat a larger model without them.
  number: +12.3, +17.5, +23.9 points; 9B with skills 47.4 vs 27B without skills 39.4
  setup: Qwen family, average over 5 benchmarks. Only 4B/9B/27B were compared, and all three sizes also differ in release version (3.5 vs 3.6).
  quote: "Qwen-3.5-9B with WikiSkill reaches 47.4% average accuracy, outperforming Qwen-3.6-27B without skills at 39.4%"
  where: p.8-9
- claim: Skills evolved by one model can beat a model's own self-evolved skills. The authors conclude that discovering skills and executing them are different capabilities.
  number: ALFWorld 70.2 vs 63.4 (Qwen-3.5-9B); SpreadSheet 50.5 vs 33.6 vs 24.3 no skill
  setup: Table 2. Skill source is Qwen-3.6-27B, Qwen-3.5-4B or Gemini-3.5-Flash. Transfer is not uniformly positive.
  quote: "Qwen-3.6-27B skills improve Qwen-3.5-9B to 50.5% on SpreadSheet, compared with 24.3% without skills and 33.6% with self-evolved skills"
  where: p.9, Table 2
- claim: Skills can transfer negatively when they encode model-specific workarounds.
  number: Gemini-3.5-Flash on SpreadSheet 50.5 -> 18.1 with Qwen-4B skills; 63.4 with Qwen-27B skills
  setup: The authors attribute it to low-level workarounds (single-line Python, string-conversion rules) and to fragmented diagnostic procedures that burn tool-call budget. This is trajectory analysis, not a controlled test.
  quote: "Qwen-3.5-4B skills reduce Gemini-3.5-Flash performance from 50.5% to 18.1%, while Qwen-3.6-27B skills improve it to 63.4%."
  where: p.9
- claim: Existing methods are less reliable. They can degrade a model that WikiSkill improves.
  number: EvoSkill on Gemma LiveMath 33.9 -> 29.8; SkillOpt on Gemini SealQA 29.4 -> 28.2
  quote: "EvoSkill improves Qwen-9B substantially on LiveMath (28.2% -> 58.1%) but degrades Gemma-4-31B on the same benchmark (33.9 % -> 29.8%)"
  where: p.8
  Also: WikiSkill is not best everywhere. EvoSkill wins LiveMath on Qwen-9B (58.1 vs 56.3), and on OfficeQA 4B, WikiSkill's own skill lowers accuracy (30.2 -> 28.5).
- claim: Large gains are concentrated in some benchmarks.
  number: Qwen-3.6-27B SpreadSheet 40.8 -> 81.7; Gemini LiveMath 33.0 -> 72.6
  setup: Test splits are small (LiveMath 124, SealQA 85, ALFWorld 134 test tasks; train 16-80, val 10-40).
  quote: "WikiSkill improves Gemini-3.5-Flash from 33.0% to 72.6% on LiveMath and from 50.5% to 76.6% on SpreadSheet"
  where: p.8; Table 6 p.20
- claim: Skill refinement is spread across iterations. Many accepted updates come late.
  number: Early/Mid/Late shares: 39-52% / 30-46% / 4-21% by model (Gemini late 4%, Qwen-4B 21%). SealQA 39/33/28.
  quote: "the initial stage accounts for 39%-52% of accepted updates, with substantial fractions continuing into the middle and late stages."
  where: p.12; Table 5 p.20. Also from Table 4: per model, about 1.2-1.6 skill creations and 0.7-1.3 edits are accepted out of 2.3-4.8 creations and 3.2-5.7 edits proposed. This is my reading of Table 4, not quoted prose.
- claim: Optimizer cost per iteration is 1+T_ReAct LLM calls, independent of training-set size.
  number: T_ReAct is roughly 10-20, so about 11-21 calls per iteration. Batch is the full training set.
  quote: "roughly10≤𝑇 ReAct≤ 20across our experiment runs"
  where: p.22, App D.2. EvoSkill is 2N/B, SkillOpt about 6-8 calls per step, Trace2Skill at least N_train. The authors concede WikiSkill "may incur higher inference cost on some datasets". No dollar or token cost is reported.

MECHANISM (for the note)
- Three layers: raw/ (immutable traces), wiki/ (patterns/, index.md, logs.md, skill-impact.md; never reset or rolled back), skills/ (SKILL.md plus PURPOSE.md linking each skill to the wiki patterns that motivated it).
- Loop per iteration:
  - Rollouts on train with the current skills; the inference agent cannot read the wiki.
  - Wiki Maintainer: up to 8 traces (max 5 failing, 3 passing), each capped at 15,000 chars. It does root-cause analysis and patch edits to pattern pages (10-30 lines each), then updates the index and appends to the log.
  - Skill Proposer: a ReAct agent with read_file. It must read at least 4 failing traces. It makes one atomic proposal to a single skill (create or patch).
  - Gate: the candidate is accepted only if validation score is strictly greater than R_best. Otherwise only the skills are rolled back and the wiki is kept.
  - The harness appends the diff, score and accept/reject outcome to skill-impact.md. The proposer prompt says "DO NOT repeat rejected approaches".
- The index entry format is "PROBLEM + ROOT CAUSE + FIX in one or two sentence", because index quality decides whether agents open the full page (Maintainer prompt, App E.2).
- Early stop if validation reaches 1.0. This happened for Gemini on ALFWorld (85.9 for all methods).
- Case study (Fig 3, Qwen-3.6-27B on ALFWorld):
  - Iteration 0: skill goal-directed-action rejected, val 0.72.
  - Iteration 1: break-repetition-loop accepted, val 0.78, informed by the rejection.
  - Iteration 4: patched with the rule "Each Operation Type ONCE Per Item".
  - This is a single illustrative case, not a measurement.

LIMITS
- Authors concede:
  - Skills are injected in full into the system prompt, so skill retrieval and triggering are not tested.
  - Strict improvement gating excludes neutral proposals that might enable later gains.
  - No automated wiki pruning, so growth over longer runs is unaddressed.
  - No very long-horizon tasks (hundreds of actions or multiple hours).
- Validation splits are small (10-40 tasks), which adds gating noise. The authors mitigate this with 3 runs, but no per-run spread is reported.
- The ablation (Table 3) is on Gemini-3.5-Flash only, covers four benchmarks, and has no ALFWorld column. The no-wiki arm removes both the wiki and the Maintainer, so the effect of the structure cannot be separated from the extra analysis LLM call (a compute confound). The authors do not discuss this.
- Baselines are re-run by the authors with matched splits. They are other people's methods, and GEPA-style prompt optimizers are not compared.
- The models and benchmarks are dated 2026 and the paper is a single-venue preprint. The Google authors use Gemini as a subject.
- The authors call the wiki "critical" and say it "persists and compounds". The only direct evidence is Table 3 and one case study.

BUILDS ON
- Karpathy (2026), "LLM Wiki" (GitHub gist), which is the stated inspiration.
- EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026), Trace2Skill (Ni et al., 2026), SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026), the three baselines.
- ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) for the proposer.
- Skills format: Anthropic (2026), Zhang et al. (2025), Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench.
- GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), acknowledged but not compared.
- Gating setup and splits follow Alzubi et al. 2026 and Yang et al. 2026.
- Related harness-evolution work: Meta-harness (Lee et al., 2026), AutoHarness (Lou et al., 2026).

CODE (verbatim, from the appendix)
- Wiki Maintainer output (App E.2):
  Return a JSON object with these keys: "create_patterns", "update_patterns" (each with "edits"), "update_index", "append_log"
  Patch ops: {"op": "append", "content": "..."}, {"op": "replace", "target": "exact text to find", "content": "..."}, {"op": "insert_after", "target": "...", "content": "..."}
- Gate (Eq. 4): S_k = S'_k if R(T_val,k) > R_best else S_{k-1}
- Algorithm 1 line 16: "Roll back skills only; wiki retained"
- Proposer finish() actions (App E.3): "create" (skill_md with YAML frontmatter + When to Apply + When NOT to Apply + Instructions; purpose_md with Origin + Patterns Addressed + Evolution History), "patch", "no_action". Rule 5: "Prefer patching existing skills over creating new ones when the existing skill is partially correct."

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): bar chart of average accuracy for No skill, EvoSkill, SkillOpt and WikiSkill on four models. It shows the gap widening with model strength.
- Fig 2 (p.4): three-layer architecture and the four-step loop (Raw is permanent and write-once; Wiki is compounding and never reset; Skills are reversible and conditional). Best single diagram for the note.
- Fig 3 (p.12): ALFWorld case study showing the wiki, log, skill-impact and skill diffs across iterations 0, 1 and 4. It shows how a rejection log steers the next proposal.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found. Extraction was clean, apart from missing spaces in some words and the table bolding being lost. Table 1 was read from the text; bold markers cannot be recovered.
- The figures.py captions command returned empty output.
- Extracted text saved at /tmp/wiki.txt (scratch only).
- Date oddity: the arXiv stamp reads 2608 (Aug 2026), consistent with the PDF header.
